source_title: Trump Played a Magic Trick on the Midwest. Is It Still Working?
source_excerpt:
A merica can be complicated, but not always. Sometimes, it is just light and darkness.
Four days ago, I was listening to Donald Trump tell a half-full arena in Youngstown, Ohio, that America is being destroyed by “low-IQ Somalis.” This was after he declared former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown “the candidate of the Marxists, the communists, and the anti-American radicals,” but before he urged a female protester being beaten by his supporters to go on a diet.
Ladies and gentlemen, we have found the darkness.
Three car rentals later — don’t ask — I am in Escanaba in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula. It has taken 12 hours. I check into my hotel and contemplate watching 48 hours straight of Brooklyn 99 and then telling my editors I’ve found nothing. But then I get out of bed and drag myself to the League of Women Voters candidate forum being held in the Escanaba city council chambers. Before going inside, I pop two Tylenol migraine pills — 65 grams each of sweet, sweet caffeine — and gird myself for the Michigan State House District 108 debate.
My phone tells me the House District 108 is 84 percent white and switched from Democratic to Republican during the Obama presidency, surely just a coincidence. The moderator asks a question about the area’s chronic battle with population loss. (The UP is twice the size of Massachusetts but has barely 300,000 residents.) The Republican candidate, a nice enough girl dad, drones on about job creation through industry growth and higher tax revenue.
I search on my phone for the nearest tavern where a man in white Stan Smiths and a BC Lions baseball cap can grab a drink without being fed into a wood chipper. The Republican is still droning. And then I hear Rachel Keys’ voice for the first time.
“They’re tripping over themselves to figure out how to fix the population, and in the meantime, in 6,000 square miles and six counties, the 108 has one place that women can go to have babies,” Keys, the Democratic candidate, says. She wears oversized glasses and dangling earrings featuring the rebel loon, a bird that has come to represent the resistance movement. “This has been an issue for the last two decades, and none of our male Republican leadership seems to think that it’s an issue.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Her confidence startles me. But 6,000 square miles for a House district? Where are we, Kamchatka? It seems impossible, so I look it up. Turns out it is quite possible.
Keys’ home is in Bay Mills on the Ojibwe reservation, just a few miles from the Canadian border. The district’s westernmost point ends in Menominee on the Wisconsin border 215 miles away. That’s four and a half hours each way on a good day, and that’s why Keys has put 27,000 miles on her car in 2026.
Back at the debate in Escanaba, I notice to the right of me a woman is scribbling out a form for the “audience asks questions” portion. I am tired and borderline irritable. I mumble to myself, “It’s going to be transgender in sports, I know it’s going to be transgender in sports, please don’t let it be transgender in sports.”
I am shushed. Turns out I was mumbling out loud.
The question: Do you think any changes should be made to the current rules for Michigan high school athletics regarding matters involving transgender student athletes participating in female sports teams? The Republican says he doesn’t understand the science but is definitely against it. Keys theatrically sighs.
“To the best of my knowledge, in the six counties that the 108 covers, there isn’t a single transgender student even trying to play sports,” says Keys. “I feel like this is just identity politics trying to take over serious issues right now. I’m a 40-year-old woman. I honestly don’t really follow high school volleyball all that much.”
“Now, I’ve been very vocal on the corporate welfare tax structure that we have; it needs to change.”
Keys is a first-time candidate in a 60-40 Republican district, so there’s not a ton of cash. She raises money for the long drives and $5 gallon gas by doing GoFundMe car karaoke. It usually nets her about a hundred bucks. Once, she made over a thousand. Then, she realized that the stylish black pantsuit with bare shoulders that she was wearing made it look like she was singing topless. She took it down.
Then there’s her source of employment. Keys’ day job is running the 180-year-old Point Iroquois Lighthouse on Lake Superior, hard on the Canadian border.
I double-check. She runs an actual lighthouse.
It is 160 miles and a three-hour drive each way from Escanaba.
I do not care. I need that lighthouse. We need that lighthouse.
Every American election is now billed as the most important one of our lifetimes. I don’t know if it’s true. I do know every election takes a little more of our souls, leaving us angrier and, somehow, more hateful.
Early in October, I made plans to hit the uber battleground states of Michigan and Ohio. I wondered whether Trump fatigue had really settled in as we headed toward the midterms. Could these two bellwether states flip from red to blue? Pundits and pollsters theorized that white working-class voters were finally realizing that Donald Trump is an expert at pushing his dirty thumb into their wounds but not actually healing them.
It makes sense. Second Term Trump is basically the president being the main character every single day on Reddit’s AmItheAsshole.
The answer is always yes. Waging war against Canada? Sure. Hiring a defense secretary in favor of public executions? Absolutely. Holding hands with Bibi and going to war with Iran? Check. Two protesters gunned down during ICE raids in Minneapolis? Affirmative.
Knock twice if you’ve heard this before. Personally, I remember reading a Rolling Stone story by some dickhead about how a 2024 Trump rally seemed tired and played out. Surely, the writer babbled, the MAGA fever was breaking in America.
The Michigan/Ohio story was my idea, and yet I was dreading it. I’d hit my personal right-wing fatigue after spending the past year writing about the murder of Melissa Hortman, getting tear-gassed in Los Angeles at an anti-ICE rally, and then being intimidated/tailgated by said ICE on suburban Minnesota roads while reporting on feds pulling over American kids on their way to high school dance class. And then I watched all six episodes of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s Great American Road Trip . In one night.
I am, as Graham Greene put it, a burnt-out case. So I put the trip off for a week and retreated to a friend’s empty house in Livingston, Montana. I needed to take in the beauty of Yellowstone and Paradise Valley, see the big sky and watch the bison roam before heading to the terror dome of the battleground state.
Then, one morning, I headed out for a walk not far from where Robert Redford filmed Where a River Runs Through It . The sky was blue, and autumn leaves rustled on quiet streets. Then, I heard gunshots and see something that looks like a tear-gas cloud. I fast-walked back home.
I opened my laptop and read that Ben Shapiro and friends are in Livingston shooting a film that makes ICE the heroes of Minneapolis. Paradise is being paved over for a Daily Wire film. I left for Youngstown, Ohio, the next day.
Second Term Trump is basically the president being the main character every single day on Reddit’s AmItheAsshole.
I’VE BEEN TO Youngstown enough that I have my favorite restaurant. Station Square Ristorante is a 40-year-old Italian joint just off I-80 and within stumbling distance of a Hampton Inn. It’s Italian old-school, something out of a Scorsese movie. I spent my 2020 Covid birthday here, downing vodka and eating ravioli at the bar, my seat partitioned from other carousers by plexiglass. A bow-tied man in a dinner jacket played tunes on a Casio keyboard.
I’ve made a point of stopping here for the night on various cross-country drives even when it didn’t make geographical sense. I never could quite put my finger on why I kept coming back until this trip. The Johnnie Walker wisdom was running high one night and it came to me: The people are happy. The food is great, the pours are strong, and they are laughing with their friends and families celebrating their nonna’s 80th birthday or Angelina and Mikey’s engagement.
This is not the vibe of the rest of Youngstown. It reminds me of Flint, Michigan, where I went to high school, a grimy and proud company town where too many promises have been broken and too many good people have moved away.
“There were so many things that were supposed to happen here,” says Marty Loney, the local union president of the Western Reserves Building Trades. “There was going to be an indoor racetrack and blimp factory. None of it ever happened.”
We’re in Loney’s office. His gray beard seems stalled in a permanent frown, which is not surprising after a lifetime in Youngstown. This election, Loney is bucking his own bosses. The statewide union has endorsed Republican Vivek Ramaswamy for governor, while Loney’s chapter is supporting Amy Acton , the Democratic nominee. Ramaswamy called Loney directly to see if he would change his mind.
“I answered the phone, he told me who he was and just started talking, then went for 10 minutes. I couldn’t get a word in,” says Loney. “Finally I said, ‘Hey, listen, you called me. Let me give you my spiel now.’ He didn’t like that idea. The last thing he said to me was, ‘If you guys would seriously consider changing your endorsement, I may come up to see you.’”
Loney’s face flushes red, and he stares at some union pins on his desk he wants to give me as a memento.
“Fuck that, I ain’t doing that. If anybody knows anything about people in Youngstown, it’s your word, your bond,” says Loney. “When you get a chance to talk to folks like that, and you see them act the way they do …” Loney trails off for a second. “Well, that’s why they have that kind of money because they screwed over too many damn people.”
“And I’m done seeing that happen to the state of Ohio.”
The question is whether the rest of Youngstown feels the same. The town has been in economic freefall for nearly 50 years since the steel mills began closing in 1977. Then came NAFTA, a global free trade treaty that made it easy for American corporations to shift well-paying blue collar jobs overseas. Union jobs in Youngstown dropped from 90,000 to 20,000 in half a century.
That’s why I’d been here before. In 2017, Lordstown, a General Motors plant 15 miles outside of Youngstown, was teetering toward closure. The plant had once employed 12,000 but now was down to 4,000. At the time, gas was cheap and Lordstown built the fuel-efficient Chevy Cruze. Everyone wanted trucks and SUVs.
That summer, Trump came to town, fresh off his first election. He boasted things were going to be different on his watch before a full house at the Cavelli Centre in downtown Youngstown.
I rode through your beautiful roads coming up from the airport. And I was looking at some of those big, once-incredible, job-producing factories, and Melania said, “What happened?” I said, “Those jobs have left Ohio . . . but they’re all coming back.” Don’t move. Don’t sell your house.”
The Lordstown plant was still savable, but Trump did nothing. Instead, he lowered federal fuel efficiency standards, leaving GM with no need for the gas-sipping Cruze. Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown — a man Trump describes as a Marxist — wrote a letter to GM CEO Mary Barra urging her to take some of the $6.9 billion the company realized in Trump tax cuts and either revive the Cruze or assign Lordstown a new car. GM never responded. The factory closed in 2019.
In my 2020 story, I traced the lives of Lordstown workers who were members of UAW 1112. Some relocated to faraway plants, some took jobs making half their pay, some fell into depression that ended in suicide. The closed GM plant went through a series of new owners, the first being Lordstown Motors, an electric car operation that brought then-Vice President Mike Pence to town.
“This is just a great day, an exciting day, where not too long ago we had heartbreaking news,” said Pence referencing the closing of the GM plant.
In the end, Lordstown Motors sold exactly 38 cars, 35 of which were recalled. The only sign that Lordstown Motors was ever here is a small slope on the property that was built for a demonstration of the company’s electric truck climbing ability. It got stuck on its only attempt.
On a beautiful October afternoon, I drive over to Lordstown to speak with the leaders of UAW 112. Their Lordstown office is huge and forlorn, built for another time. Now it’s a historic relic, a Mangiot Line fort that the Germans just blitzed on their way to Paris.
I sit down at a conference table with George Gorantis, the current president of UAW 1112, and Josh Johnson, a UAW man in his thirties. Gorantis jokes that Johnson had been present at the closing of the last three steel mills operating in Ohio, eliciting a laugh from Josh Ayers, the burly shop chairman at Ultium Cells.
Ultium is a new plant building batteries for electric cars that GM funded as a consolation prize for Lordstown after the Cruze was discontinued. Understandably, the trio are more eager to talk about the battery plant than reopen old Lordstown GM wounds.
And they have a right to be proud; the UAW has achieved great things for their workers. The plant opened in 2022, with workers initially earning $16.50, less than could be made at a nearby Amazon distribution center. Safety procedures were lax and workers began quitting, uncertain of how their interaction with acid and liquids in the production process might impact their future health.
But then Gorantis and the national UAW went to work. In June 2024, the UAW and the plant reached an agreement that upped wages to $35 an hour by the end of the contract. Safety stewards were hired, and things were looking up.
“You could just see in the parking lots, people were doing better,” says Gorantis. “People had new or newer cars that didn’t break down and sit in the lot. They could quit their second jobs.”
Shortly after the June agreement was reached, UAW 1112 members faced another challenge. Donald Trump of “don’t sell your houses” fame was campaigning for president again. He spoke long and loud about his hatred of electric vehicles. It bordered on the pathological. He promised to dismantle the policies encouraging Americans to buy them, including a $7,500 federal rebate available to new buyers.
This wasn’t complicated: If Trump was reelected in 2024, the electric car business would suffer along with battery plants like Ultium Cells. And that’s exactly what happened. Trump eliminated the electric car incentives, and sales dived. In January 2026, over 1,300 union workers were laid off from Ultium.
I ask the trio if they had impressed on their members the importance of not voting for the guy who had a visceral hatred of their industry just for self-preservation reasons.
The room goes silent for a moment. Then Ayers, the UAW shop steward at Ultium Cells, speaks up.
“I’m an old-school conservative Democrat,” says Johnson. “My parents, my grandfather are all Democrats, but this new woke shit. I don’t like it. I don’t like all this bullshit they talk about.”
“I voted for Harris, but I did vote for Trump in 2016.”
“There was a belief that under the Biden administration, the inflation, the cost of things, was going up,” says Ayers, tugging at his baseball cap. “I think there was a hope that there would be a repeat cycle of when Trump was in office in ‘16 to ‘20. Unfortunately, it’s not working out that way.”
“I don’t regret it,” says Ayers. He cites his support for Trump’s wars against Iran and Venezuela as good things. He mentions Trump’s promise that we would be soon harvesting Venezuela’s oil reserves. “It could be a great thing,” says Ayers.
We make small talk, and Gorgantis mentions that Ultium Cells is now bringing back a lot of their workers who had been laid off in January.
I want to say that it would have been even better if they had not been laid off to begin with, but it seems pointless. Instead, I shake their hands and then climb into my gas-powered 2026 SUV rental and drive away.
I share my UAW encounter with other people in Youngstown, without mentioning the specific shop. I ask former Sen. Brown, who is now running for Senate again, at a Youngstown campaign stop about Democrats meeting resistance in once favorable places where culture issues still seem to supplant personal well-being. (He’d just been to the UAW 1112 office a week earlier.)
“You win them back by talking to them, by listening to them, as I always have,” says Brown. “By going to their plant, going to their churches, going to their town halls, and listening to people. And how are we going to fight back? Voters didn’t vote for this war. They didn’t vote for higher grocery prices. They didn’t vote for gas prices to go up $1. Farmers didn’t vote for and truckers didn’t vote for diesel prices to double.”
It is a politician’s answer, probably smart with two weeks to go.
Marty Loney just sighs when I tell him about my other Youngstown encounters. He mentions an analogy he uses with his members.
“Here we are, 10 years later, no further ahead, right?” says Loney. “So we’ve gone through those lies and those promises, and that’s exactly what we’re getting here again. Let me ask you a question: If your wife made all the money in the world, and came home and lied to you every minute of the day, every day of the week, would you still be married to her?”
It’s a good metaphor, but I kept finding people in Youngstown willing to stay in an abusive relationship.
“Here we are, 10 years later, no further ahead, right? So we’ve gone through those lies and those promises, and that’s exactly what we’re getting here again.”
BUT MAYBE FEWER of them. The Covelli Centre in downtown Youngstown was filled with nearly 7,000 people in 2017 for Trump’s “”don’t sell your homes” rally. But now it is October 2026, and the thrill is gone. The back portion of the arena is blocked off by a giant American flag. Other sections with perfect views of the stage are empty. Charitably, there’s maybe 3,500 people here.
I should point out I’ve been to too many Trump rallies. There was the Covid-infested Tulsa rally of 2020 (RIP Herman Cain) and, more recently, the 2024 Return to Butler rally where Elon Musk jumped up and down like a spastic robot being fed the wrong voltage. Still, today is easily the saddest.
The event kicks off with Republican state treasurer candidate Jay Edwards offering the invocation.
“Lord, thank you for the Mahoning Valley, for the steelworkers, and the union families who never gave up on this place, even when the mills went quiet. Lord, let the furnaces roar again.”
Edwards recently represented a district 175 miles to the south, so maybe he doesn’t know that Youngstown’s last blast furnace was dismantled in 2017. There is no place for it to roar.
Eventually, Youngstown congressman Michael Rulli walks to the podium. He reminds everyone that it is Columbus Day and thanks Christ we are free to celebrate Columbus again even if the explorer never actually set foot on mainland America. (OK, I added that last part.)
“Last weekend, I was on the plane with the president on Air Force One, and he says, ‘I have a special surprise for you, Rulli,’ he says, ‘I’m coming to Youngstown because I didn’t forget them.’”
The crowd cheers, perhaps not realizing that the question isn’t whether Donald Trump has forgotten they exist, but whether he has done anything for them.
Ramaswamy speaks next. He swears Ohio will soon, economically, make Texas and Florida jealous. He offers no details. He moves to more comfortable ground.
“As Americans, we believe in merit — that the best person gets the job regardless of their skin color,” says Ramaswamy. He then steals from MLK. “That you are judged not on the color of your skin, but on the content of your character and your contributions.”
(A week later, the content of Ramaswamy’s character is revealed when he airs an attack ad against Amy Acton featuring Acton’s mother, a woman who abandoned her daughter in 1978, sticking with her husband, a man indicted for sexually assaulting Acton when she was a child.)
Eventually, Trump emerges to the Lee Greenwood song and begins by praising the physical attributes of Republican Sen. Jon Husted .
“I looked at his ass, and I looked at the whole, and then I looked at his hands. Look at his hands! He’s got these claws.”
Trump then turns to what he believes is Ohio’s most pressing problems: the 60,000 Somalis who make up 0.5 percent of the state’s population.
He plays dumb about the recent raid on Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home but describes her as a “disaster.” He then cites a series of crimes in Minnesota that may or may not have involved Somali Americans.
“This is not what we want in this country,” says Trump.
“Somalia, they love Mercedes,” says Trump. “They come in, they have nothing, and they’re the number-one buyers of Mercedes-Benz and BMWs in the state of Minnesota. The whole thing is crazy. It’s crazy, low-IQ people.”
Trump then brings up Springfield, Ohio, 200 miles away. That’s where Ohio native J.D. Vance declared Haitian Americans were eating the cats and dogs of their neighbors, a charge that Vance admitted later was complete bullshit.
“If you want to stop Ohio from being plundered, ransacked, and destroyed like Minnesota’s being destroyed — we’re going to stop it just like we did with Springfield.”
At one point, a female protester stands up and starts shouting about the Epstein files. The Trump crowd does not wait for security. I watch them punch the woman in the face and chest.
Trump smiles. He then gets the protester’s gender wrong.
“Oh, he’s got to go on a diet. He’s a fat guy. Wow. Wow. Got to go on a diet fast.”
It is not until 40 minutes in that Trump begins to brag about what he has done for Youngstown.
“The big steel company, Vallourec, is investing $48 million to expand operations right here in a place called Youngstown.”
A few days later, Jobs Ohio — a state economic development corporation — reports that once operational the new Vallourec project will create 40 jobs.
A few minutes later, Trump begins raging about “the transgender mutilization of your children.”
My serotonin levels are crashing, and the only thing that can help is a Station Square stop. Last call is 9 p.m. I jog out to my car. There’s a problem. Security for Trump’s motorcade has already cut off my exit ramp. I am screwed. Then I see a dirt path at the back of my parking lot used for maintenance vehicles.
Fuck it. I head down the rutted road at 40 mph. My high beams terrorize two rabbits, and they scurry for the ditch. I emerge a half mile away under an overpass. I then run some very yellow lights pulling into the restaurant with 20 minutes to spare.
I grab a barstool and order pumpkin ravioli and down a vodka on the rocks. Next to me are two men. We will call the older one Rosencranz and the younger man Guildenstern. Rosencranz sees my press pass. He asks me if I went to the rally. I say yes. He sees the name of my publication and elbows Guildenstern.
“We were gonna go
